paragraphs.source_en: Whereas the relationship of the lithic industry with the engravings is only hypothetical, a more precise chronological assessment might be provided by the examination and dating of the patina. The term "patina" or "rock varnish" indicates a dark coating covering stable, aerially exposed rock surfaces in arid lands. It consists mainly of clay minerals, manganese and iron oxides deposited on rocks under wet environmental conditions (Cremaschi 1996). In the Messak Plateau in Libya the organic matter trapped in rock varnish layers during their deposition was AMS radiocarbon dated showing that no pre-Holocene patina had been deposited (Zerboni 2008). The Messak varnish consisted of micro layers resulting from biogeochemical processes acting at different time during the Early and Middle Holocene.

paragraphs.source_en: The innermost layer formed between 9,200 and 5,500 BP, the second layer between 6,000 and 4,000 BP and the upper one before 3,400 BP. These three micro layers were formed by different processes which record a climatic transition from a wet environment to progressively arid conditions.

paragraphs.source_en: In the Central Sahara a direct relationship exists between the age of varnish development and the engravings, the darker the patina the older the engravings. The examination of the patina, combined with the dating of archaeological remains found under patinated stone structures in the Messak, indicates that the main formation of the desert varnish in this region occurred between 6,100 and 5,100 BP (Cremaschi 1996; Mori 2000). Therefore this is the ante quem limit for all fully patinated engravings in this region, however it must be pointed out that the spatial distribution and formation of rock varnish was probably irregular, responding to different geographical settings on the Plateau (Zerboni 2008). At all sites the patina stopped forming at around 3,400 BP, which is the ante quem limit for all patinated engravings in the Central Sahara.
